item.title: Kansas Judge Dismisses Murder Charge Against Sheriff’s Deputy
item.description:
A Kansas judge dismissed a murder case on Thursday against a sheriff’s deputy who was accused last year of fatally kneeling on a handcuffed inmate, the county prosecutor’s office and the deputy’s lawyer said.

Prosecutors indicated that they would appeal the judge’s decision to drop all charges against the deputy, Richard Fatherley, who had been accused of second-degree murder in the July 2025 death of Charles Adair at the jail in Kansas City, Kan.

The death of Mr. Adair, who had been arrested based on misdemeanor warrants related to traffic tickets, prompted outcry last year in the Kansas City region and is the subject of an unresolved federal lawsuit.

Mr. Adair, who used a wheelchair and had several medical problems, was being wheeled back to his cell after having a dressing on his leg rewrapped when he got into a dispute with a deputy, according to an affidavit filed in court. Mr. Adair at that point threw himself out of his wheelchair, the filing said. He was then handcuffed, put back in the chair and wheeled to his cell, where deputies placed him on the bottom bunk, the affidavit said.

Mr. Adair, who remained handcuffed, was heard yelling “help,” the affidavit said. Deputy Fatherley then approached Mr. Adair and put his left knee on Mr. Adair’s lower back, while other Wyandotte County deputies held down other parts of his body, according to the affidavit.

Deputy Fatherley continued to hold Mr. Adair down until shortly after the handcuffs were removed, the affidavit said. A nurse soon entered the cell, where Mr. Adair was found to be unresponsive, the affidavit said. He was later pronounced dead, and an autopsy classified the death as a homicide.

The Kansas City Star reported on Thursday that Judge Aaron Roberts found that prosecutors had not met their burden for the case to proceed from a preliminary hearing to a trial. A written ruling from Judge Roberts, of the State District Court in Wyandotte County, was not immediately published on the court docket.

James L. Spies, a lawyer for Deputy Fatherley, said his client was “tremendously relieved” by the judge’s decision.

“My client never set out to harm him, never set out to do wrong by Mr. Adair,” Mr. Spies said.

The district attorney’s office in Wyandotte County said in an unsigned statement that it had already filed a notice of appeal.

“We respect the law, but disagree with the decision,” the statement said.

An attempt to reach lawyers for the Adair family was not immediately successful.

item.title: Los Angeles Mayor, Stung in Debate, Eases Street Vending Crackdown
item.description:
Mayor Karen Bass has eased a crackdown on Los Angeles street vendors after she compared them with homeless encampments last week, setting off fierce criticism and creating a flashpoint in her re-election campaign.

During a heated debate with Nithya Raman, a progressive Democrat whom Ms. Bass will face in November’s election, the mayor said that she did not believe that vendors should be allowed to sell food in front of restaurants.

“I do not think that you should have a food vendor in front of a restaurant. Period,” Ms. Bass said, suggesting that the vendors should be restricted to certain locations, and, eventually, move into brick-and-mortar facilities.

“You can move that person so that person can have a living, make money, but not right in front of a restaurant that discourages patrons from going in,” she said. “Just like you shouldn’t have encampments in front of restaurants, or in front of schools.”

The comments angered some vendors and others who criticized Ms. Bass for conflating them with homeless people. They said the comment showed that the mayor was out of touch with what many consider to be one of the most beloved parts of Los Angeles’s food culture.

“These are individuals who are moms, who are our uncles, who work legitimately, who wake up really early,” said Sergio Jimenez, who has organized with street vendors across Los Angeles for close to a decade.

“They’re not addicts. They’re not taking funds from the government,” he said, adding that many had fought for years to legalize parts of their industry. “It was like a slap in the face,” he said.

Across the sprawling city, vendors serve tamales from coolers, assemble flame-roasted meat on hot tortillas and grill bacon-wrapped sausages until crispy. They pop up on corners, in parking lots and outside grocery stores. Some have folding tables for patrons. Their food is far cheaper than what many restaurants offer. Yet many are just as well known and beloved — with lines often stretching down the road.

Historically, street vending has also been an easily accessible profession for new immigrants who may not have the resources to open a brick-and-mortar shop, and they offer a familiar taste of home to Angelenos far from their home countries.

Under state law, sidewalk vending is decriminalized, though vendors must follow local regulations and obtain permits. But advocates say that the police have sometimes used an anti-camping ordinance to issue citations to vendors at MacArthur Park, a hub in one of Los Angeles’s most immigrant-heavy neighborhoods. Mr. Jimenez said he had worked with about a dozen vendors who he believed had been wrongly cited.

In a statement on Thursday, Ms. Bass’s office said she “stands firmly with street vendors” and had directed the Los Angeles Police Department to stop issuing them criminal citations, and to dismiss those issued in error, “ensuring they are not left with criminal records for working to provide for their families.”

Paige Sterling, a spokeswoman for Ms. Bass, said that the police had informed Ms. Bass’s office that criminal citations had been issued in error around MacArthur Park. The mayor’s office has asked the police to confirm that the issue was not more widespread, the spokeswoman said.

“Street vending is a quintessential part of L.A.’s world-class food scene and a livelihood for thousands of hard-working Angelenos,” her office said, noting that it had spent nearly $500,000 this fiscal year on a joint program with Los Angeles County that helps vendors establish or grow their businesses.

The Los Angeles Police Department did not immediately respond to a request seeking more information on Thursday.

The dispute has further highlighted the divide between Ms. Bass, 72, a nationally known Democrat who has struggled to rebound since the Los Angeles wildfires, and Ms. Raman, a City Council member and former Bass ally who has drawn comparisons to New York’s democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

In recent months, the two candidates have clashed over policing, housing and homelessness — all evidence of an ideological and generational divide between the center-left Democratic establishment that has shaped the city for years, and young progressives. Ms. Raman, 44, has described the vendors as among the most vibrant and visible parts of the city’s economy.

In 2024, Ms. Raman backed a measure reducing the city’s vending permit fee to $27.51 from $541. She has criticized state laws and a confusing process that stops many stands from getting the health permits they need to operate legally.

Speaking at a taco stand on Wednesday, Ms. Raman said Ms. Bass “took a shot at street vendors” but that she planned to work with them to regulate and legalize operations.

Mr. Jimenez said that while there was a long way to go toward improving conditions, the news that the police would stop issuing criminal citations to vendors was “a positive step.”

item.title: Judge Once Again Bars Postal Service From Restricting Mail-In Vote
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday once again temporarily prohibited the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan to restrict mail-in voting, put in place after a directive from President Trump.

Federal District Judge Indira Talwani had cleared the way for the Postal Service to move forward just the day before, but on Thursday, she issued a new order concluding that the agency’s plan, released late on Friday, appeared to overstep its legal mandate and could spark chaos by changing rules fewer than 70 days before an election.

She wrote that a group of Democratic-led states that had sued “face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away.”

“Most plaintiff states have already ordered their mail ballots, and some are required by state law to send them to eligible voters as early as next week,” she added.

She wrote that while the Supreme Court had “admonished” her on Monday that the Postal Service had not finalized any changes when the groups sued initially, making court action premature, the stakes had changed since then because of the step the agency took Friday to formalize its plan.

Her ruling marked the third court decision on the issue in less than a week, a whipsaw of action that threatened to confuse voters. But each delay has reduced the administration’s chances of clearing the legal hurdles to execute its logistically complicated mail-in ballot plan before the November election. She blocked the rule from taking effect for 14 days, and she had previously scheduled a hearing to discuss the legality of the rule on Sept. 3.

In her order, Judge Talwani explained that the prospect of the new rule suddenly taking effect carried “significant risk of their members’ disenfranchisement” for voting rights organizations, which had also sued, along with the states.

She ticked through a list of requirements that state election officials would be required to meet to ensure delivery of ballots, including receiving the agency’s approval for new envelope designs and submitting voters’ information into an online portal run by the Postal Service.

“Where a state or local election official does not obtain envelope and return envelope design approval, or does not upload voter information, or does not include unique intelligent mail bar codes on ballot envelopes, the U.S.P.S. will not mail ballots to voters,” she concluded.

In March, President Trump issued an executive order that required the Department of Homeland Security to create and circulate state-by-state citizenship lists to state officials. It further urged states to provide the U.S. Postal Service with their own lists of voters eligible to cast ballots by mail.

Multiple lawsuits were filed challenging the order, arguing that Congress and the states set rules for elections, not the executive branch. The challengers also argued that no federal law gives the Postal Service the power to make those kinds of election-related rules.

On Monday, the Supreme Court ruled that one suit, brought by a group of Democratic-led states, was premature because the administration had not started implementing its plans.

But late Friday, just before the court ruled, the Postal Service formally published a new plan to comply with the executive order. Under that plan, the service would not deliver mail ballots in states that do not share voter data with the agency and would only deliver ballots that meet certain criteria.

Lawyers for the Trump administration and the groups challenging the rule continue to clash over a straightforward issue: Whether or not the Postal Service’s plan would mean the agency would be taking on a new role verifying voters and potentially rejecting ballots in the midterm election in November.

In a filing on Thursday, the Postal Service denied that its proposal left room for the service to second-guess states on which voters were eligible to cast a ballot.

“U.S.P.S. will not scrutinize those decisions or alter that information in any way — instead leaving it entirely up to the states to accurately and lawfully identify its residents who are eligible to vote by mail,” the filing said. “The Postal Service will not determine voter eligibility, ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures.”

Instead, it described the changes as minor logistical improvements and streamlining, such as requiring voters to submit their addresses ahead of time to improve processing. It said the changes were designed “as a matter of the Postal Service’s own judgment.” Lawyers for the service argued it is authorized to adopt mail rules under statutes adopted by Congress.

A spokesman for the Postal Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The challengers argue that the Postal Service rule is an unconstitutional violation of the separation of powers, allowing the executive branch to intrude into elections. They say that no federal law permits such action by the agency, and they assert that the Trump administration’s actions are likely to sow confusion among voters and to lead to disenfranchisement.

The agency has said that it would not try to impose the new requirements for the 2026 elections, unless explicitly allowed to by the courts.

A series of lawsuits in Massachusetts and the District of Columbia by different groups have challenged Mr. Trump’s effort to discredit and erect obstacles to mail-in voting. The lawsuits have challenged both Mr. Trump’s executive order and the Postal Service rule, focusing on their implementation this year and beyond.

Adam Sella contributed reporting.

item.title: The Town Council Race Was Tied. The Three of Spades Called It.
item.description:
There was an old-fashioned Wild West standoff this week in a onetime frontier outpost.

Two candidates for Town Council in Gila Bend, Ariz., finished with the same number of votes in July’s election, 67 each. A century-old state law mandated breaking the tie with a game of chance.

In this duel, there would be no gunslinging, though there would be a draw — not from a holster, but from a shuffled deck of cards. The hopeful with the higher card would claim the seat.

In an age of increasing distrust in elections and a state that has been a hotbed for voting-related conspiracy theories, Gila Bend’s leaders said they knew the high-stakes tiebreaker, which took place Tuesday, would need to be transparent and carefully choreographed.

“With everything that’s going on, you want it as open as you can possibly get it,” said Patricia Riggs, the town clerk, who oversees elections.

The stalemate in this 1,800-person community, 50 miles southwest of Phoenix, was hardly the first to be decided by chance in a country with tens of thousands of elected local governments and closely divided politics. Races in recent decades have come down to poker games, straw-drawing and, earlier this month in Hawaii, names tucked into plastic eggs and picked from a woven basket.

But Gila Bend’s tie might have been the first involving a candidate who had been in the exact same position years before. Jesus Rubalcava finished neck and neck with an opponent in 2014 and won his first term on the Council with the flip of a $1 coin.

After a court-certified recount earlier this month confirmed his deadlock with the newcomer Athena Guerrero, Ms. Riggs informed Mr. Rubalcava that his election fate would once again come down to chance.

Did that make him lucky or unlucky? Mr. Rubalcava, a high school teacher and former state legislator, wasn’t sure.

“I was in disbelief,” he said. “I couldn’t wrap my head around it.”

It was up to Ms. Riggs and other town officials to choose what form the rubber match would take. Arizona law stipulated only that the tie be broken “by lot.” They ruled out rock-paper-scissors, and they opted against drawing marbles or straws.

“We thought that was kind of boring,” Ms. Riggs said.

High-card draw would be more exciting, they decided, and it would be easy for the public to understand and follow.

Ms. Guerrero was initially wary. “I’m not a gambling type of person,” she said.

But she knew enough to pray for an ace. Ms. Guerrero, who works for a water treatment plant, had long eyed politics, and she imagined the Town Council as a launching pad. Eventually, she said, she would like to be mayor.

Gila Bend, an important stop on a storied 19th-century stagecoach line, is now a manufacturing and farming town where local politics is unavoidably personal. In separate interviews, Ms. Guerrero and Mr. Rubalcava each said they “have nothing but love” for the other.

Neither campaigned aggressively, and the nail-biter was a reminder that every vote counts. Mr. Rubalcava’s mother, brother and niece all failed to cast ballots, he said.

They were not alone. Fewer than 200 of the town’s roughly 600 registered voters participated in the July election.

Ms. Riggs spent three weeks painstakingly planning Tuesday’s showdown, consulting with lawyers and election experts. She devised a list of 19 steps that documented exactly how the draw would go, and she wrote a script to read while she conducted it.

On Tuesday morning, she borrowed a mechanical card shuffler from her sister-in-law and bought two decks at the town’s Dollar General, one for practice. That night, the two candidates sidled up to a table in a school building and exchanged nervous smiles in front of a handful of residents and the sitting Council members.

Ms. Riggs stated the rules, opened and spread a new deck of cards and let Ms. Guerrero and Mr. Rubalcava inspect them. She shuffled and presented the stack to Ms. Guerrero, who cut it. Mr. Rubalcava then cut it again.

The candidates were reminded that, in the event they drew the same number — like that would ever happen — spades would trump other suits.

Ms. Riggs pulled Ms. Guerrero’s card first, a three of clubs. The candidate sighed.

Ms. Riggs flipped Mr. Rubalcava’s card next.

Another three, another tie. The audience gasped. Mr. Rubacalva couldn’t believe it. “Did this really just happen?” he thought.

But his three was a spade, delivering Mr. Rubalcava a chance victory for the second time. The candidates laughed and shook hands.

“Who would have thought?” a stunned Ms. Riggs said to the room.

Ms. Guerrero said on Wednesday that she planned to run for office again, pledging to “come back strong in a couple years.”

Ms. Riggs said she was glad to hear it, then added: “God forbid there’s a tie.”

item.title: With Term Winding Down, Pelosi Tries to Anoint a Successor
item.description:
Nancy Pelosi has a meaty to-do list in her final months in office: Ensure Democrats take back the House of Representatives. Fend off attempts by the Trump administration to make it harder to vote in the midterms.

And persuade San Franciscans to send a local elected leader little known outside the city to replace her in Washington.

Ms. Pelosi, 86, who is finishing her final term in Congress after representing San Francisco since 1987, has never been one to sit back and watch politics play out. This particular campaign is no exception.

She has engaged in the race to a surprising degree, considering that she did not seem to have longstanding ties with her preferred candidate, Connie Chan, a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. Still, Ms. Pelosi has publicly inserted herself in the race and has worked vigorously behind the scenes to get Ms. Chan elected.

Ms. Chan and her opponent, State Senator Scott Wiener, will square off Nov. 3 in an intraparty battle. Like most San Franciscans, both candidates are liberal Democrats and share a disdain for the Trump administration, as well as a desire to expand rights for immigrants and gay and transgender people.

But they represent different camps in the city’s combative political scene, particularly on housing. Mr. Wiener, 56, has gained national attention as a prolific state legislator focused on getting as much housing as possible built. Ms. Chan, 47, has a reputation in San Francisco for regularly blocking housing proposals, which she sees as lining the pockets of developers to the detriment of low-income tenants who could be displaced.

He calls her an obstructionist best known for voting “no,” saying she is trying to keep San Francisco frozen in amber. She calls him beholden to corporations and billionaires.

Enter Ms. Pelosi.

The first woman to serve as the speaker of the House, she stayed out of the primary campaign until the final two weeks, when she endorsed Ms. Chan. Since then, she has hosted a fund-raiser in the Jackson Square neighborhood for Ms. Chan, lent her communications director to Ms. Chan’s campaign and worked the phones to gather endorsements, including an unsuccessful attempt to convince the labor leader Dolores Huerta to endorse both candidates, not just Mr. Wiener.

Mr. Wiener’s camp believes Ms. Pelosi has been motivated less by wanting to elevate Ms. Chan than by seeking to block him from the seat he has long coveted. It was well known in California political circles that he had been eyeing Ms. Pelosi’s seat for years, and he had once vowed not to run until she announced her retirement.

Last October, however, Mr. Wiener refused to wait any longer and jumped into the race before Ms. Pelosi announced her decision.

Ms. Pelosi has given few interviews about the congressional race. But she said this week that her support for Ms. Chan had nothing to do with her feelings about Mr. Wiener.

“Nobody knows Congress better than I do. Nobody,” Ms. Pelosi said. “And I think she would be the best member of Congress.”

Ms. Pelosi answered questions about the race after an event at San Francisco City Hall to herald the 106th anniversary of the certification of the 19th Amendment, which established the right to vote for women.

There, she listed several reasons for her involvement: Ms. Chan is a woman at a time when women are losing political power. The two have long ties to the city’s powerful labor unions. Ms. Chan performed well as the chairwoman of the board’s budget committee. And Ms. Chan worked hard to help pass Proposition 50, the 2025 ballot measure that gerrymandered California’s congressional map to the benefit of Democrats in response to a similar move in Texas that aided Republicans.

The only negative word Ms. Pelosi would say this week about Mr. Wiener was to reiterate her anger over a satirical chatbot his campaign created that was intended to parrot Ms. Chan and always say “no.”

The stunt backfired when supporters of Ms. Chan, who moved to San Francisco from Hong Kong when she was 13, typed in topics not related to policies, such as the word “accent.” The bot responded with lines that included, “I’m afraid my San Francisco accent is so thick I can barely understand myself.”

Ms. Pelosi released an open letter co-signed by numerous San Francisco female politicians and political groups saying that the chatbot relied on “racist, misogynist tropes for cheap political points.” Mr. Wiener apologized and took the chatbot down.

A group of prominent women who support Mr. Wiener held a rally last weekend in Alamo Square to denounce what they viewed as false outrage over the chatbot and promote his record of legislation important to women, including to expand reproductive freedom and health care access.

Susie Tompkins Buell, founder of the Esprit clothing company and a Democratic power broker in California, spoke at the rally and said in an interview later that she was confused about why Ms. Pelosi was going all-in for a less experienced candidate.

“It’s not about any woman. It’s about the right woman,” she said. “Connie Chan is a place where progress goes to die.”

This week, Ms. Pelosi said she held no ill will against Mr. Wiener for anything other than the chatbot.

“I haven’t said anything about her opponent except when he tried to put words in the mouth of a woman, which is something that I have been fighting to protect my whole career,” Ms. Pelosi said.

Some in San Francisco political circles have speculated that Ms. Pelosi was frustrated with Mr. Wiener because his candidacy might have edged out her own daughter, Christine Pelosi, from running for her seat. But Ms. Pelosi said this week that she and her daughter had never talked about a succession plan; Christine Pelosi is now running to fill Mr. Wiener’s seat in the State Senate.

“She wants to have her own path in California, which I love,” Ms. Pelosi said. “There was never any thought that she would run for my seat, although they like to use that because they don’t know what they’re talking about.”

Christine Pelosi, who was at the City Hall event wearing a tiny pin of a famous image of her mother in a red coat and sunglasses, reiterated that she had never planned to run for Congress and added that she, too, was supporting Ms. Chan. “With respect, some of us do things for positive reasons,” Christine Pelosi said.

In an interview, Ms. Chan said she and Ms. Pelosi have talked often in recent months, and that the congresswoman has been generous with her advice. Ms. Chan described filming the endorsement video together as a pinch-me moment.

“Deep inside me, I was thinking, ‘Oh, I only wish my mother was still alive to see this,’” she said.

Mr. Wiener said in an interview that the chatter about Ms. Pelosi’s involvement was a distraction.

“I’m not running against Nancy Pelosi. I’m running against Connie Chan,” he said. “And I’m going to win.”

item.title: Wyoming Governor Objects to ‘Very Odd’ D.O.J. Election Monitoring
item.description:
Two election monitors from the Justice Department tried to interview voters and examine voting machines at polling places during Wyoming’s primaries last week, local officials said, drawing pushback from the state’s Republican governor.

The federal election monitors arrived at a polling site in Cheyenne, Wyoming’s capital and its largest city, without advance notice around 7 a.m. last Tuesday, said the Laramie County clerk, Debra Lee. They asked to interview voters and inspect the machines, but were denied, officials said.

“It was aggressive, unexpected, disruptive — certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state,” Gov. Mark Gordon of Wyoming said in an interview on Thursday. “We’re going to get to the bottom of it as best we can.”

The Justice Department often monitors polling sites during elections. But the visits to Wyoming came amid President Trump’s ongoing fixation with finding evidence of fraud and vote tampering. Mr. Trump and his allies made fantastical claims that voting machines had switched votes for him to his opponent Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2020, and he has tried and failed to find evidence of widespread fraud or vote tampering ever since.

Mr. Trump has often returned to such conspiracy theories in his second term, arguing that widespread fraud could affect this year’s elections. As president, he has deployed the resources of the federal government, notably the Justice Department’s, to investigate his unsubstantiated claims, sowing more doubt in the nation’s elections and raising alarm among state officials about whether he will try to intervene if Republicans lose their congressional majorities in November.

Governor Gordon, a low-key, term-limited Republican who leads one of the country’s most conservative states, said at a meeting with state election officials on Wednesday that he had been concerned by the behavior of the election observers.

“I feel very strongly about the federal government coming in and taking our guns — I don’t like that,” Mr. Gordon said at the meeting. “And I don’t like the federal government coming in and taking our votes, either.”

The monitors ultimately visited six polling places, showing their credentials only when asked for them, Mr. Gordon said in the interview, describing their behavior as “very odd.” He said he had asked the state attorney general, Keith Kautz, to investigate the matter.

The observers had cited statutes related to the Americans With Disabilities Act and the Civil Rights Act, Mr. Gordon said.

This year, the Justice Department’s observers have visited polling places in other states, including politically tense regions such as the Minneapolis area. The agency said on Tuesday that it had sent 80 monitors to seven states during primary season.

But the requests to interview voters and gain access to machines in Wyoming were unusual. And they come at a moment when the Justice Department has been locked in an intense legal battle with roughly 30 states, demanding their private, unredacted voter rolls in a hunt for evidence of noncitizen voting.

In early July, the Justice Department sent letters to every state and Washington, warning that top election officials would be criminally prosecuted if they allowed ballots to be cast by noncitizens.

The monitors in Wyoming said they had been sent to assess whether the election was in compliance with federal civil rights and voting rights laws, Ms. Lee said. But their questions appeared to be “outside the scope of federal voting rights laws,” she said in a statement.

“They included questions about the nature, length and timing of poll worker training,” Ms. Lee said. “Monitors requested training guides, asked how our new election equipment was acquired and wanted to examine our tabulators.”

Their conduct, Ms. Lee said, displayed a “complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections.”

Mr. Trump has filled the Justice Department and other federal agencies with officials sympathetic to his baseless claims about the 2020 election. In Georgia, the focus of many of Mr. Trump’s efforts to reverse the 2020 election, the F.B.I. this summer assigned a team to examine 2020 records seized from Fulton County, home of Atlanta.

The office of the U.S. attorney in Wyoming, Darin D. Smith, did not immediately respond to questions about the election monitors’ appearance. But in a statement provided by the Justice Department’s Washington office, Mr. Smith said that voters deserved “absolute confidence that their ballots are secure and their voices are heard without interference.”

“We are working alongside local officials to ensure every lawful vote is protected,” Mr. Smith said in the statement.

At the meeting on Wednesday, Mr. Gordon told Chuck Gray, the Wyoming secretary of state, that he did not believe the U.S. attorney’s office in Wyoming was aware that the Justice Department observers would be visiting.

But Mr. Gray, who once claimed the 2020 presidential election was “illegitimate,” told the governor that he understood that Mr. Smith had been given advance notice about the observers.

Mr. Gray said that “Wyoming election law does provide for observation.”

A spokeswoman for the Justice Department, Kiersten Pels, said Mr. Smith had been given advance notice.

Ms. Lee, the county clerk, said in her statement that a Justice Department official had told her the decision to deploy monitors to Wyoming was made on short notice. The Justice Department issued a statement on the day of the state’s primary saying that it was deploying observers to Wyoming and Florida to ensure “transparency, ballot security and compliance with federal law.”

Although many of the Justice Department’s monitoring efforts have been uneventful, a letter it sent in June to election officials in Wayne County, Mich., which includes Detroit, became a flashpoint.

The letter described polling sites with machines that were not working and at least one site with a shortage of provisional ballots. It drew a scathing response from Janice Winfrey, the Detroit city clerk.

“It is important to address election performance based on facts rather than falsehoods that lead to baseless conclusions,” Ms. Winfrey said in a letter sent to Justice Department officials in July. She added that the department’s assertions form “a baseless conclusion that then becomes the pretext for additional monitoring of Detroit elections.”

Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

item.title: Jury Deliberations Underway in Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial
item.description:
Jury deliberations are set to resume on Friday morning in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murder for strangling her three young children in 2023.

After more than four weeks of often emotional testimony in the high-profile case, the lawyers on each side made their closing arguments at the courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday. It was their final opportunity to convince the jurors whether or not Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the children’s deaths.

Ms. Clancy does not deny that she killed the children at her home in Duxbury, Mass., an affluent Boston suburb, and has pursued an insanity defense. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, maintains that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and had experienced auditory hallucinations of a man’s voice ordering her to kill her children and then herself.

Mr. Reddington described Ms. Clancy on Thursday as “a darn good mother” and a respected nurse who loved her children. He read from a long list of medications that had been prescribed to Ms. Clancy in the months before the killings, arguing that she had received “lousy medical care” when she sought help for her anxiety.

“This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children,” Mr. Reddington said, “because she was suffering from a disease and defect.”

Earlier on Thursday, the judge, William Sullivan of Plymouth County Superior Court, had told the jurors that Ms. Clancy could not be held criminally responsible if she had a mental disease or defect that prevented her from controlling her actions, or from distinguishing right from wrong.

Jennifer Sprague, a prosecutor, used her closing argument to present the killings as a series of rationally made and premeditated choices. She called the killings an act of “extreme atrocity and cruelty” and described the horrific scene that Ms. Clancy had left behind.

“She left them discarded on the basement floor, like broken toys, because she was done playing the game,” Ms. Sprague said. “You know, to a moral certainty, she is guilty.”

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Clancy plotted to get her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house on Jan. 24, 2023. Mr. Clancy returned home from picking up takeout food to find the children in the basement with exercise bands around their necks, he said during his testimony. Cora, 5, and Dawson, 3, were dead. Callan, 8 months, died days later.

Mr. Clancy also found Ms. Clancy lying injured in the backyard. She had cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window of the home in what her lawyers have called a suicide attempt, which left her partially paralyzed.

Ms. Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. The witnesses have included Ms. Clancy’s mother, her sister, her former mother-in-law, and several psychologists who treated Ms. Clancy before the killings or evaluated her afterward. The prosecution rested early last week after calling more than 70 witnesses, and the defense rested on Friday after calling 10.

Rebuttals, which give prosecutors an opportunity to respond to claims made by the defense, took up the last few days of the trial. The three rebuttal witnesses for the prosecution, all forensic psychologists, pointed to evidence that Ms. Clancy may not have been suffering from postpartum psychosis. In combative cross-examinations, Mr. Reddington questioned their expertise and at one point asked the judge to grant a mistrial after one of the witnesses mentioned the concept of “mortal sin” while discussing Ms. Clancy’s Catholic upbringing.

For much of the trial, a crowd of demonstrators has gathered outside the courtroom. Many were women who wore pink to support Ms. Clancy and to call attention to what they see as the health care system’s failures to address maternal mental health.

In her closing argument, Ms. Sprague said that the case was “not about our mental health system, or how it treats women.”

She added: “That’s a distraction to get you angry and passionate — about an important issue, but an issue that’s not on trial here.”

To secure a guilty verdict, the prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Clancy committed the crime, knew that the murders were wrong and had some control over her actions.

Judge Sullivan instructed the jury to choose among first-degree murder, second-degree murder and manslaughter if they find Ms. Clancy guilty. She faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.
